w: עַל כָּךְ שֶׁ|over the fact that|~fixed phrase
s.line: Dorothy wept bitterly at the passing of her hope to get home to Kansas again;
s.note: בְּמָרִירוּת = "bitterly", from מַר (bitter): בְּ + an abstract noun is a common way to make an adverb (בְּשִׂמְחָה, בְּכָבוֹד). אָבְדָה תִּקְוָה (hope was lost) may ring a bell: Israel's anthem has עוֹד לֹא אָבְדָה תִקְוָתֵנוּ, "our hope is not yet lost".

w: בְּכַדּוּר פּוֹרֵחַ|in a balloon|~lit. a flying ball
s.line: but when she thought it all over she was glad she had not gone up in a balloon.

w: וְכָךְ גַּם|and so did|~fixed phrase: and so also
s.line: And she also felt sorry at losing Oz, and so did her companions.
s.note: A binyan pair: pa'al אָבַד = "got lost, was lost" (the hope in sentence 1), pi'el אִבֵּד = "lost (something)": אִבַּדְתִּי אֶת הַמַּפְתְּחוֹת (I lost the keys). הִצְטַעֵר (to be sorry, to regret) is hitpa'el: after צ the ת of the prefix swaps places and becomes ט. אֲנִי מִצְטַעֵר is the everyday "I'm sorry".

s.line: The Tin Woodman came to her and said:
“Truly I should be ungrateful if I failed to mourn for the man who gave me my lovely heart.
s.note: הָיִיתִי + participle = "I would …": הָיִיתִי מִתְאַבֵּל (I would mourn). כְּפוּי טוֹבָה is the set phrase for "ungrateful"; feminine כְּפוּיַת טוֹבָה. The opposite is מַכִּיר טוֹבָה or, very commonly, אֲסִיר תּוֹדָה (grateful).

s.line: I should like to cry a little because Oz is gone,
if you will kindly wipe away my tears, so that I shall not rust.”
s.note: תִּהְיִי נֶחְמָדָה וּ… + future ("be nice and …") is how Israelis make a polite request: תִּהְיֶה נֶחְמָד וְתַעֲבִיר לִי אֶת הַמֶּלַח (would you pass me the salt). לִי here means "for me", and it does the job of "my": תְּנַגְּבִי לִי אֶת הַדְּמָעוֹת = wipe my tears. הֶחְלִיד (to rust) is hif'il; חָלוּד = rusty.

s.line: “With pleasure,” she answered, and brought a towel at once.
s.note: בְּשִׂמְחָה = "gladly, with pleasure", the standard friendly yes to a request; in slang you will also hear בְּכֵיף. הֵבִיא (brought) is the hif'il of בָּא (came): "made come".

s.line: Then the Tin Woodman wept for several minutes,
and she watched the tears carefully and wiped them away with the towel.
s.note: הִשְׂגִּיחַ עַל = to keep watch over, supervise. A מַשְׂגִּיחַ is a supervisor, especially the kashrut inspector in a restaurant. אוֹתָן is feminine plural because דְּמָעוֹת is feminine. נִגֵּב (to wipe) and מַגֶּבֶת (towel) share the root נ־ג־ב.

w: בְּאַבְנֵי חֵן|with jewels|~lit. stones of grace
לְיֶתֶר בִּטָּחוֹן|to be on the safe side|~idiom: for extra safety
s.line: When he had finished, he thanked her kindly and oiled himself thoroughly with his jeweled oil-can, to guard against mishap.
s.note: הוֹדָה לְ־ = to thank (someone), the same root as תּוֹדָה. מְשֻׁבָּץ is the pu'al of שִׁבֵּץ (to set in, to fit into a slot); today שִׁבֵּץ also means to schedule or assign someone to a shift. לְיֶתֶר בִּטָּחוֹן = "just to be safe", a very common phrase.

s.line: The Scarecrow was now the ruler of the Emerald City,

w: וְאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁ|and although|~fixed phrase
s.line: and although he was not a Wizard the people were proud of him.
s.note: אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁ = "although"; in everyday speech לַמְרוֹת שֶׁ is more common. גֵּאֶה בְּ־ = proud of, with בְּ: אֲנִי גֵּאָה בְּךָ (I'm proud of you).

s.line: “For,” they said, “there is not another city in all the world that is ruled by a stuffed man.”
s.note: שָׁלַט בְּ־ = to rule over, to control. Hebrew turns Baum's passive ("is ruled by") into an active verb. The same root gives שַׁלִּיט (ruler) and שַׁלָּט, which today means both a sign and a TV remote. מְמֻלָּא (stuffed) is a pu'al participle, as in פִּלְפֵּל מְמֻלָּא (stuffed pepper).

w: וְעַד כַּמָּה שֶׁ|and as far as|~fixed phrase
s.line: And, so far as they knew, they were quite right.
s.note: "To be right" is a verb in Hebrew: צָדַק, אַתָּה צוֹדֵק (you're right), הִיא צוֹדֶקֶת. עַד כַּמָּה שֶׁ… = "as far as …": עַד כַּמָּה שֶׁיָּדוּעַ לִי (as far as I know).

s.line: The morning after the balloon had gone up with Oz, the four travelers met in the Throne Room and talked matters over.
s.note: פָּגַשׁ אֶת (pa'al) = to meet someone; נִפְגַּשׁ (nif'al) = to meet each other: נִפָּגֵשׁ מָחָר (let's meet tomorrow). אַרְבַּעַת הַ… is the construct form of the number, meaning "the four …".

s.line: The Scarecrow sat in the big throne and the others stood respectfully before him.

w: מָה שֶׁבָּא לָנוּ|what we please|~idiom: lit. what comes to us
s.line: “We are not so unlucky,” said the new ruler, “for this Palace and the Emerald City belong to us, and we can do just as we please.
s.note: חֲסַר + noun = "without, lacking": חֲסַר מַזָּל (unlucky), חֲסַר סַבְלָנוּת (impatient); the plural is חַסְרֵי. בָּא לִי = "I feel like": בָּא לִי גְּלִידָה (I feel like ice cream), לֹא בָּא לִי (I don't feel like it).

s.line: When I remember that a short time ago I was up on a pole in a farmer’s cornfield,
s.note: זָכַר (pa'al) = to remember, keep in mind; נִזְכַּר (nif'al, active meaning) = to recall, suddenly remember: פִּתְאֹם נִזְכַּרְתִּי (suddenly I remembered). לִפְנֵי + a time = "… ago": לִפְנֵי שָׁבוּעַ (a week ago).

s.line: and that now I am the ruler of this beautiful City, I am quite satisfied with my lot.”
s.note: מְרֻצֶּה = satisfied, the pu'al participle of רִצָּה (to satisfy, appease); it takes מִ־: מְרֻצֶּה מִ…. Without vowels, מרצה can also be מַרְצֶה, a lecturer.

s.line: “I also,” said the Tin Woodman, “am well-pleased with my new heart;
and, really, that was the only thing I wished in all the world.”
s.note: יָחִיד = only, single, sole: בֵּן יָחִיד (an only son). It comes after the noun like any adjective: הַדָּבָר הַיָּחִיד (the only thing).

s.line: “For my part, I am content in knowing I am as brave as any beast that ever lived, if not braver,” said the Lion modestly.
s.note: מִבְּחִינָתִי = "as far as I'm concerned", very common in speech: מִבְּחִינָתִי אֵין בְּעָיָה (it's fine by me). חַיָּה (animal) and חָיְתָה (she lived) come from the same root ח־י־ה.

s.line: “If Dorothy would only be contented to live in the Emerald City,” continued the Scarecrow, “we might all be happy together.”
s.note: אִלּוּ opens an unreal "if": אִלּוּ + הָיְתָה …, then הָיִינוּ + participle in the result ("we would …"). מוּכָן (ready, willing) is a hof'al participle, "made ready", from the root כ־ו־ן.

s.line: “But I don’t want to live here,” cried Dorothy.
“I want to go to Kansas, and live with Aunt Em and Uncle Henry.”
“Well, then, what can be done?” inquired the Woodman.
s.note: אֶפְשָׁר + infinitive, with no subject, = "one can / it can be done": מָה אֶפְשָׁר לַעֲשׂוֹת? = what can be done? Its opposite is אִי אֶפְשָׁר (impossible).

s.line: The Scarecrow decided to think, and he thought so hard that the pins and needles began to stick out of his brains.
s.note: כָּל כָּךְ … שֶׁ… = "so … that …": הָיָה כָּל כָּךְ חַם שֶׁלֹּא יָצָאנוּ (it was so hot that we didn't go out). הֶחְלִיט (decided) is hif'il; the noun is הַחְלָטָה (a decision).

s.line: Finally he said:
“Why not call the Winged Monkeys, and ask them to carry you over the desert?”
s.note: לָמָּה שֶׁלֹּא + future = "why don't we / why not …?": לָמָּה שֶׁלֹּא נֵלֵךְ לַיָּם? (why don't we go to the beach?). בִּקֵּשׁ מִ־ = to ask of someone, with מִ־: בִּקַּשְׁתִּי מִמֶּנּוּ (I asked him).

w: לֹא עָלָה עַל דַּעְתִּי|never occurred to me|~idiom: lit. did not go up on my mind
s.line: “I never thought of that!” said Dorothy joyfully.
s.note: עָלָה עַל דַּעְתּוֹ = "it occurred to him", lit. "it went up on his mind". It is very often negative: זֶה לֹא עָלָה עַל דַּעְתִּי (it never crossed my mind). The idea is the subject: רַעְיוֹן עָלָה עַל דַּעְתָּהּ (an idea occurred to her).

s.line: “It’s just the thing.
I’ll go at once for the Golden Cap.”
s.note: For something you are about to do right now, Hebrew often uses the present: <t>אֲנִי הוֹלֶכֶת</t> = "I'm going / I'll go". <t>הוֹלֶכֶת</t> is feminine because Dorothy is speaking.

s.line: When she brought it into the Throne Room she spoke the magic words,
and soon the band of Winged Monkeys flew in through the open window and stood beside her.
s.note: לַהֲקָה = a band or flock of animals, and also a music band or dance troupe. It is feminine singular, so the verbs are עָפָה and עָמְדָה, even though there are many monkeys. עַד מְהֵרָה = "soon, before long", a bookish but still common phrase.

s.line: “This is the second time you have called us,” said the Monkey King, bowing before the little girl.
s.note: זוֹ הַפַּעַם הַשְּׁנִיָּה שֶׁ… = "this is the second time that …". פַּעַם is feminine, hence זוֹ and הַשְּׁנִיָּה. Hebrew uses the present (קוֹרֵאת) where English says "you have called". קָרָא לְ־ = to call (someone).

s.line: “What do you wish?”
s.note: רְצוֹנֵךְ = "your wish" (feminine "your"), from רָצוֹן (will, wish). מָה רְצוֹנְךָ? is a polite, slightly formal "what do you wish?"; in normal speech you would say מָה אַתְּ רוֹצָה?.

s.line: “I want you to fly with me to Kansas,” said Dorothy.
s.note: "I want you to …" is אֲנִי רוֹצָה שֶׁ… + future: אֲנִי רוֹצָה שֶׁתָּבוֹא (I want you to come). Hebrew has no "want + someone + to-infinitive" construction.

s.line: But the Monkey King shook his head.
s.note: הֵנִיעַ אֶת רֹאשׁוֹ לִשְׁלִילָה = shook his head "no"; nodding "yes" is לְחִיּוּב. שְׁלִילָה and חִיּוּב are also the words for "negative" and "positive" in grammar and in argument.

s.line: “That cannot be done,” he said.
“We belong to this country alone, and cannot leave it.
s.note: אוֹתָהּ (it, feminine) because אֶרֶץ is feminine, as are most country names: יִשְׂרָאֵל יָפָה.

s.line: There has never been a Winged Monkey in Kansas yet, and I suppose there never will be, for they don’t belong there.
s.note: הִנִּיחַ (present מַנִּיחַ) = to suppose, assume; it also means "to put down": הִנַּחְתִּי אֶת הַסֵּפֶר עַל הַשֻּׁלְחָן. The noun הֲנָחָה means both "an assumption" and "a discount" in a shop.

s.line: We shall be glad to serve you in any way in our power, but we cannot cross the desert.
s.note: נִשְׂמַח לְ… + infinitive = "we'll be glad to …", a phrase you will meet in every customer-service message: נִשְׂמַח לַעֲזֹר (we'll be happy to help). בִּיכָלְתֵּנוּ = "in our ability", from יְכֹלֶת (ability).

s.line: Good-bye.”
And with another bow, the Monkey King spread his wings and flew away through the window,
s.note: פָּרַשׂ (spread out) is written with שׂ. Without dots it looks just like פָּרַשׁ, with שׁ, which means "retired, withdrew": הוּא פָּרַשׁ לְגִמְלָאוֹת (he retired on a pension).

s.line: followed by all his band.

w: עַל סַף|on the verge of|~idiom: on the threshold of
s.line: Dorothy was ready to cry with disappointment.
s.note: עַל סַף = "on the threshold of, on the verge of", a favorite of news headlines: עַל סַף מִלְחָמָה (on the brink of war), עַל סַף פְּשִׁיטַת רֶגֶל (on the verge of bankruptcy).

s.line: “I have wasted the charm of the Golden Cap to no purpose,” she said, “for the Winged Monkeys cannot help me.”
s.note: סְתָם = "for nothing, pointlessly", and in speech also "just, for no reason": סְתָם שָׁאַלְתִּי (I was just asking), סְתָם! (just kidding!). בִּזְבֵּז (to waste) is a four-letter root in pi'el.

s.line: “It is certainly too bad!” said the tender-hearted Woodman.
s.note: חֲבָל = "too bad, what a pity": חֲבָל שֶׁלֹּא בָּאתָ (too bad you didn't come). Slang twist: חֲבָל עַל הַזְּמַן ("a pity about the time") is praise, "amazing!". רַךְ הַלֵּב: adjective + noun in construct, "soft of heart".

s.line: The Scarecrow was thinking again, and his head bulged out so horribly that Dorothy feared it would burst.
s.note: One root, two binyanim: pa'al פָּחַד = to be afraid, hif'il הִפְחִיד = to frighten, so מַפְחִיד = scary. After פָּחֲדָה שֶׁ… the verb is future, as usual after fearing. הִתְפּוֹצֵץ = to burst, explode; הִתְנַפֵּחַ = to swell up (נִפַּח = to blow up a balloon).

s.line: “Let us call in the soldier with the green whiskers,” he said, “and ask his advice.”
s.note: בּוֹאוּ + future (נִקְרָא) = "let's …": בּוֹאוּ נֵלֵךְ (let's go). עֵצָה = a piece of advice; הִתְיַעֵץ עִם = to consult with someone, from the same root.

s.line: So the soldier was summoned and entered the Throne Room timidly,
s.note: זֻמַּן = "was summoned", the pu'al of pi'el זִמֵּן (to summon, call in). The hif'il הִזְמִין is the everyday verb "to invite, to order": הִזְמַנּוּ פִּיצָה (we ordered pizza).

s.line: for while Oz was alive he never was allowed to come farther than the door.
s.note: הִרְשָׁה (hif'il) = to allow; הֻרְשָׁה (hof'al) = was allowed: לֹא הֻרְשָׁה לוֹ = he was not allowed. Hebrew says "it was not allowed to him". כָּל עוֹד = "as long as, while".

s.line: “This little girl,” said the Scarecrow to the soldier, “wishes to cross the desert.
How can she do so?”

w: אֵין לִי מֻשָּׂג|I have no idea|~idiom
s.line: “I cannot tell,” answered the soldier, “for nobody has ever crossed the desert, unless it is Oz himself.”
s.note: אֵין לִי מֻשָּׂג = "I have no idea", the everyday way to say "I can't tell". אַף אֶחָד אַף פַּעַם לֹא stacks the negatives, as in Hebrew it must. חוּץ מִ־ = except for.

s.line: “Is there no one who can help me?” asked Dorothy earnestly.
“Glinda might,” he suggested.
s.note: הִצִּיעַ = to suggest, to offer; the noun is הַצָּעָה (a suggestion, an offer). It also has a homely meaning: הִצִּיעַ אֶת הַמִּטָּה = made the bed.

s.line: “Who is Glinda?” inquired the Scarecrow.
s.note: מִי זֹאת? / מִי זֶה?: in "who is …?" the pronoun follows the gender of the person asked about. זֹאת because Glinda is a woman.

s.line: “The Witch of the South.
She is the most powerful of all the Witches, and rules over the Quadlings.
s.note: The superlative: adjective + בְּיוֹתֵר = "the most …": הַחֲזָקָה בְּיוֹתֵר (the most powerful). In speech you will more often hear הֲכִי before the adjective: הֲכִי חֲזָקָה.

s.line: Besides, her castle stands on the edge of the desert, so she may know a way to cross it.”
s.note: חוּץ מִזֶּה = "besides, apart from that", very common in speech. בִּקְצֵה is בְּ + the construct of קָצֶה (edge, end): בִּקְצֵה הָרְחוֹב (at the end of the street).

s.line: “Glinda is a Good Witch, isn’t she?” asked the child.
s.note: …, נָכוֹן? ("…, right?") is the all-purpose Hebrew tag question. It never changes, where English needs "isn't she / aren't they / didn't he".

s.line: “The Quadlings think she is good,” said the soldier, “and she is kind to everyone.
I have heard that Glinda is a beautiful woman, who knows how to keep young in spite of the many years she has lived.”
s.note: לַמְרוֹת + noun = "in spite of, despite": לַמְרוֹת הַגֶּשֶׁם (despite the rain); before a clause it is לַמְרוֹת שֶׁ…. נִשְׁאַר (to stay, remain) is nif'al with an active meaning; its infinitive is לְהִשָּׁאֵר.

s.line: “How can I get to her castle?” asked Dorothy.
s.note: אֵיךְ מַגִּיעִים לְ…? is how you ask for directions: אֵיךְ מַגִּיעִים לַתַּחֲנָה? (how do you get to the station?). הִגִּיעַ (to arrive, reach) is hif'il, root נ־ג־ע.

s.line: “The road is straight to the South,” he answered, “but it is said to be full of dangers to travelers.
s.note: דָּרוֹמָה = "southward": the ending ָה marks direction, as in הַבַּיְתָה (homeward) and צָפוֹנָה (northward). אוֹמְרִים שֶׁ…, a plural verb with no subject, = "people say, it is said". דֶּרֶךְ is feminine, so הוֹלֶכֶת and מְלֵאָה.

w: חַיּוֹת פֶּרֶא|wild beasts|~lit. animals of wildness
s.line: There are wild beasts in the woods, and a race of queer men who do not like strangers to cross their country.
s.note: חַיַּת פֶּרֶא (plural חַיּוֹת פֶּרֶא) = a wild animal. In construct only the first noun changes: חַיָּה → חַיַּת, חַיּוֹת stays. זָר = a stranger, a foreigner; it also means "foreign": שָׂפָה זָרָה (a foreign language).

s.line: For this reason none of the Quadlings ever come to the Emerald City.”
s.note: מִסִּבָּה זוֹ = "for this reason", a written, news-style phrase. In conversation you would say בִּגְלַל זֶה or לָכֵן.

s.line: The soldier then left them and the Scarecrow said:
“It seems, in spite of dangers, that the best thing Dorothy can do is to travel to the Land of the South and ask Glinda to help her.
s.note: נִרְאֶה שֶׁ… with no subject = "it seems that …". הֲכִי + adjective is the everyday superlative: הַדָּבָר הֲכִי טוֹב (the best thing). בִּקֵּשׁ מִמִּישֶׁהוּ שֶׁ… + future = to ask someone to do something.

s.line: For, of course, if Dorothy stays here she will never get back to Kansas.”
“You must have been thinking again,” remarked the Tin Woodman.
s.note: כַּנִּרְאֶה = "apparently, evidently", from נִרְאֶה (seems). It does the work of English "must have": כַּנִּרְאֶה שָׁכַחְתִּי (I must have forgotten).

s.line: “I have,” said the Scarecrow.
s.note: To answer "yes" to a question or remark, Hebrew often just repeats the verb: <t>חָשַׁבְתָּ?</t> <t>חָשַׁבְתִּי.</t> English does the same with its helper verb ("I have").

w: נִמְאַס לִי|I am tired|~idiom: nif'al · מ־א־ס
s.line: “I shall go with Dorothy,” declared the Lion, “for I am tired of your city and long for the woods and the country again.
s.note: נִמְאַס לִי מִ־ = "I'm fed up with", where the thing is the subject and you are לִי. הִתְגַּעְגֵּעַ לְ־ = to miss, to long for, with לְ: אֲנִי מִתְגַּעְגֵּעַ אֵלַיִךְ (I miss you). הִכְרִיז (declared) is a news word too: הַכְרָזָה = an announcement.

s.line: I am really a wild beast, you know.
Besides, Dorothy will need someone to protect her.”
s.note: הִצְטָרֵךְ = to need, hitpa'el with the ת switched to ט after צ, like הִצְטַעֵר. הֵגֵן עַל = to protect, with עַל; מָגֵן דָּוִד (the Star of David) comes from the same root.

s.line: “That is true,” agreed the Woodman.
“My axe may be of service to her;
s.note: עָשׂוּי לְ… + infinitive = "may, is likely to", a slightly formal phrase: הַמְּחִירִים עֲשׂוּיִים לַעֲלוֹת (prices may rise). In other contexts עָשׂוּי מִ־ means "made of". הוֹעִיל = to be useful; מוֹעִיל = useful.

s.line: so I also will go with her to the Land of the South.”

w: יוֹצְאִים לַדֶּרֶךְ|do we set out|~idiom: lit. go out to the road
s.line: “When shall we start?” asked the Scarecrow.
s.note: יָצָא לַדֶּרֶךְ = to set out on a journey. The plural present with no subject (יוֹצְאִים) is a natural way to say "when are we leaving?"

s.line: “Are you going?” they asked, in surprise.
“Certainly.

w: הָיָה לִי|I would have had|~lit. there would be to me
s.line: If it wasn’t for Dorothy I should never have had brains.
s.note: אִלְמָלֵא + noun = "if not for, but for": אִלְמָלֵא הָעֶזְרָה שֶׁלְּךָ (if it weren't for your help). It belongs to written Hebrew; in speech people say אִם לֹא … or בְּלִי …

s.line: She lifted me from the pole in the cornfield and brought me to the Emerald City.
s.note: הוֹרִיד (took down) is the hif'il of יָרַד (went down): "made go down". Today it also means to download: הוֹרַדְתִּי אֶת הָאַפְּלִיקַצְיָה.

w: אַחַת וּלְתָמִיד|for good and all|~idiom: once and for always
s.line: So my good luck is all due to her, and I shall never leave her until she starts back to Kansas for good and all.”
s.note: חַיָּב usually means "must", but חַיָּב לְ־ + a thing = "owe": אַתָּה חַיָּב לִי כֶּסֶף (you owe me money). אַחַת וּלְתָמִיד = "once and for all".

w: בְּהַכָּרַת תּוֹדָה|gratefully|~lit. with recognition of thanks
s.line: “Thank you,” said Dorothy gratefully.
s.note: הַכָּרַת תּוֹדָה = gratitude, lit. "recognition of thanks", from הִכִּיר (to know, recognize). Someone grateful is מַכִּיר טוֹבָה.

s.line: “You are all very kind to me.

w: כַּמָּה שֶׁיּוֹתֵר מַהֵר|as soon as possible|~fixed phrase: as much as more fast
s.line: But I should like to start as soon as possible.”
s.note: כַּמָּה שֶׁיּוֹתֵר + adjective/adverb = "as … as possible": כַּמָּה שֶׁיּוֹתֵר מַהֵר (ASAP), כַּמָּה שֶׁיּוֹתֵר אֲנָשִׁים (as many people as possible).

s.line: “We shall go tomorrow morning,” returned the Scarecrow.
s.note: הֵשִׁיב = to reply (a more formal עָנָה); it is the hif'il of שָׁב (returned), so it can also mean "to give back": הֵשִׁיב אֶת הַכֶּסֶף. The noun is תְּשׁוּבָה (an answer).

s.line: “So now let us all get ready, for it will be a long journey.”
s.note: הִתְכּוֹנֵן = to get ready, prepare oneself, from the root כ־ו־ן, like מוּכָן (ready). מַסָּע = a journey, a trek; the root נ־ס־ע also gives נָסַע (to travel).
